title: The fight over the Siang dam
dek: Villages along the Siang oppose an 11,000 MW dam that would submerge 27 villages. Four villagers held since 9 October were freed on 7 November; six others remain detained.

story.text: The Siang Upper Multipurpose Project is an 11,000 MW hydropower plant being developed by NHPC. Mongabay India reports it would submerge 27 villages, including Yingkiong, Upper Siang's district headquarters, and residents of Siang, Upper Siang and East Siang districts have consistently opposed it.
story.takeaway: The 11,000 MW dam, built by NHPC, would submerge 27 villages, Mongabay India reports, and residents have long opposed it.

story.text: The current protests oppose a pre-feasibility study by NHPC at the proposed dam sites, one of the last studies before the dam's detailed project report. Early this month protests turned violent: protesters set fire to vehicles and stormed an MLA's house, and police allegedly lathi-charged protesters on 4 October.
story.takeaway: Today's protests target the pre-feasibility study, one of the last steps before the dam's detailed project report.

story.text: On 9 October four villagers of Geku, Adum Tayom, Omak Paron, Okut Paloh and Oson Paron, were detained under the Arunachal Pradesh Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 2014; their lawyer says the families at first received only notices. On 11 October the district banned gatherings of five or more people, and on 14 October a sessions court gave 13 people named in two police cases interim protection from arrest.

On 22 October opponents began a 24-hour sit-in at Miracle Ground in Pasighat, demanding an end to survey work, the release of those held and the withdrawal of central armed police. The district allowed it but barred any march beyond the ground. Five more activists were reportedly taken into custody in Pasighat; associates said they did not know where they were held.

On 23 October a 12-hour bandh was called across Siang, Upper Siang and East Siang. At Dite-Dime near Geku, police fired tear gas and four to five women were hospitalised; a cameraman was reportedly hit by a shell. That night protesters reportedly set fire to an NHPC office, a police station and police vehicles in Pasighat, and vandalised the homes of local political leaders. The unrest continued until about 4am on 24 October. Protesters want 10 arrested activists freed and an independent inquiry into the police action.

On 24 October shops in Pasighat stayed shut. Police detained five youths for questioning over the vandalism of homes, and from 5pm gatherings of more than five people were barred in Pasighat, Mebo and Ruksin. Arunachal Times reports five police personnel and several protesters were injured in the clashes. Activists and lawyers, among them human rights lawyer Ebo Mili, surrendered to police, saying the bandh had been peaceful and young people were not behind the violence.

On 25 October prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the BNSS stayed in force in parts of East Siang, and officials reported no fresh violence. Chief Minister Pema Khandu met the Arunachal Indigenous Tribes Forum and other community organisations, and convened MLAs from all parties to discuss the pre-feasibility report and survey. Protest groups' demands include scrapping the project, withdrawing armed forces, releasing 10 arrested activists and reinstating suspended village chiefs.

On 26 October East Siang police said 26 people, five of them juveniles, had been arrested over the 23 October violence in Pasighat, and six more detained for questioning; eight cases are registered under the BNS and the public property damage law. The same day, activists Ebo Mili and Otul Jerang, in police custody since surrendering, reportedly began a hunger strike.

On 27 October ThePrint reported that 30 companies of central armed police are deployed across East Siang, Siang and Upper Siang, and the district magistrate said the Section 163 curbs on gatherings in Pasighat, Mebo and Ruksin will stay "until further orders". Ebo Mili's family said his health, with hypertension and diabetes, is deteriorating in custody and asked for proper medical care; he and Otul Jerang have distanced themselves from the arson.

On 27 October the inspector-general of police for the central range, Hibu Tamang, said 69 people had been arrested and four detained under the Arunachal Pradesh Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act over the 23 October violence, with 55 cases registered across Upper Siang, Siang and East Siang. They face charges of rioting, burning vehicles and damaging property; Ebo Mili and Otul Jerang say they took no part in the arson. On 28 October rural development minister Ojing Tasing said he had met representatives of 72 villages in East Siang, and that the concerns and rights of local communities must remain central to decisions on the project.

On 29 October The Federal reported Hibu Tamang's count as 53 cases (26 in Upper Siang, 21 in Siang and 6 in East Siang) and 69 arrests, with notices under the BNSS served on more than 200 people. The Siang Indigenous Farmers' Forum said it will not meet Chief Minister Pema Khandu until those jailed are released and army and paramilitary forces leave Siang and Upper Siang. The same day, protesters in traditional dress marched against the dam, demanding the release of those in custody and the withdrawal of cases.

On 30 October a group of citizens protested outside Nehru Park in Guwahati, Assam, against the Upper Siang project and the proposed Lower Siang project, demanding the unconditional release of arrested Adi leaders and protesters. Journalist Maini Mahanta, who spoke, condemned the arrests of protesters and journalists; a protester claimed about 26,000 trees had been felled for the project. No official response to the Guwahati protest was reported.

On 31 October Delhi Police detained protesters, including activist Katon Moyong (known as Abor Man), at a solidarity protest outside Arunachal Bhawan in New Delhi that demanded the project's withdrawal, the release of detainees and the removal of central forces. Organisers Himkhand said about 40 were detained and alleged that some were sexually assaulted while being put into buses; some were later released. No Delhi Police response to the allegations was reported. The same day the Arunachal Indigenous Tribes Forum formed a seven-member peace committee to facilitate dialogue among all stakeholders.

On 2 November the Siang Indigenous Farmers Forum and the SUMP Affected Area Youth Association began a 36-hour shutdown across three districts, demanding the release of people detained over the agitation and a halt to pre-feasibility work on the Siang. Shops and petrol pumps in Yingkiong stayed shut, and internet services were suspended in Yingkiong, Simong, Komkar and Geku "to curb the spread of misinformation through social media"; no bandh-related incidents were reported in the district. Forum president Nobeng Burang said the agitation would end if the government released the detained.

In a statement to the Adi community, Chief Minister Pema Khandu said: "We are not talking about dam construction at this stage." He said neither the Union nor the state government had decided to build the project, that the pre-feasibility report "is not a final approval", and that decisions would come "only through open discussion and with your consent". The report did not mention the detained.

On 5 November the Siang Indigenous Farmers' Forum turned down the chief minister's invitation to talks in Itanagar between 5 and 7 November, set out in a 3 November letter from his office. The forum said it "will not engage in discussions with the government unless all detainees are released and armed forces are withdrawn." Separately, the Adi Galo Welfare Society began a foot march from Geku to Itanagar on 4 November with the same demands, reaching Bodak in East Siang on 5 November. No government response to either was reported.

On 7 November the four Geku villagers held since 9 October under the state's anti-terror law, Adum Tayom, Omak Paron, Okut Paloh and Oson Paron, were released from Jully Central Jail near Itanagar, officials said. The state had agreed a day earlier to free them as a goodwill gesture in reply to the farmers' forum's demands, and approved reinstating suspended village heads. It said withdrawing FIRs must follow due legal process and that pulling out central forces would be discussed at talks with the chief minister. Six others remain in detention, PTI reported.

official.text: The detention orders cite violence, arson and public safety. Police say protesters at Dite-Dime threw stones and defied prohibitory orders; on 27 October the police inspector-general said those arrested face charges of rioting, burning vehicles and damaging property. Chief Minister Pema Khandu offered talks ("The government's doors are always open") and says the dam is mainly meant to store water in view of China's planned dam upstream. On 28 October minister Ojing Tasing said the project needs people's trust and called for transparency and dialogue. No police comment on the hunger strike was reported. On 29 October the state government said current work is only technical and environmental surveys for a feasibility report; the chief minister says the government will protect national interests while respecting Siang Valley residents' rights. No Delhi Police response to the 31 October allegations was reported. On 2 November Chief Minister Pema Khandu said: "We are not talking about dam construction at this stage", adding that decisions would come only with people's consent; internet services in parts of Upper Siang were suspended "to curb the spread of misinformation". On 3 November the chief minister's office invited the Siang Indigenous Farmers' Forum to talks in Itanagar on 5–7 November; no government response to the forum's refusal was reported. On 6 November the state agreed to release the four detained villagers as a goodwill gesture, said withdrawing FIRs must follow due legal process, and invited the forum to talks with the chief minister.

On 9 October four Geku villagers were detained under the state's anti-terror law, and gatherings were banned. On 22 October opponents held a 24-hour sit-in in Pasighat; five more activists were reportedly taken into custody.

On 23 October police fired tear gas during a bandh and four to five women were hospitalised. That night an NHPC office, a police station and vehicles in Pasighat were reportedly set on fire. Protesters want 10 arrested activists freed. On 24 October five youths were detained, gatherings were barred in Pasighat, and lawyer Ebo Mili and other activists surrendered to police.

seo_title: Siang dam protests, Arunachal: detentions, releases, talks offer

whats_new.text: Four Geku villagers held under the state anti-terror law since 9 Oct were freed on 7 Nov as a state "goodwill gesture"; six others remain detained, PTI reported. The state invited talks.

summary.label: What's happening
summary.text: Adi villages along the Siang oppose an 11,000 MW dam that would submerge 27 villages; protests turned to arson in Pasighat on 23 October.

summary.label: Why it matters
summary.text: Police say 69 were arrested under the state anti-terror law; four villagers were freed on 7 November, six remain held.

summary.label: What's next
summary.text: The state invited the farmers' forum to talks with the chief minister; a foot march heads for Itanagar.
